# Git Merge vs Git Rebase

## What They Do

**`git merge`** combines two branches by creating a new "merge commit" that has two parents, preserving the exact history of how branches diverged and came back together.

**`git rebase`** moves or replays your commits on top of another branch, rewriting history to appear as if you branched from a different point.

---

## Visual Comparison

**Starting state:**
```
main:    A --- B --- C
                \
feature:         D --- E
```

**After `git merge main` (from feature):**
```
main:    A --- B --- C
                \       \
feature:         D --- E --- M   ← merge commit (has 2 parents)
```

**After `git rebase main` (from feature):**
```
main:    A --- B --- C
                         \
feature:                  D' --- E'   ← commits replayed, new hashes
```

---

## Key Differences

| Aspect | Merge | Rebase |
|--------|-------|--------|
| History | Preserves exact history | Rewrites history (new commit hashes) |
| Merge commit | Yes, creates one | No extra commits |
| Conflicts | Resolved once | Resolved per-commit being replayed |
| Safety | Safe on shared branches | **Dangerous on shared branches** |
| Traceability | Shows when/where branches diverged | Linear, harder to see original branch point |

---

## When to Use Each

### Use `merge` when:
- Working on **shared/public branches** (main, develop)
- You want to **preserve the true history** of when work happened
- Merging a completed feature back into main
- Working with a team and others have pulled your branch

```bash
# Standard feature branch workflow
git checkout main
git merge feature/my-feature
```

### Use `rebase` when:
- **Updating a local feature branch** with latest changes from main
- You want a **clean, linear history** before merging
- Cleaning up messy local commits before sharing (`rebase -i`)
- Working on a **private branch** nobody else has

```bash
# Keep your feature branch current
git checkout feature/my-feature
git rebase main

# Interactive rebase to clean up commits
git rebase -i HEAD~3
```

---

## The Golden Rule

> **Never rebase commits that have been pushed to a shared repository**

When you rebase, commits get new SHA hashes. If others have based work on the old commits, their history diverges from yours, causing serious problems.

```bash
# DANGEROUS if others have pulled this branch
git push origin feature
git rebase main          # rewrites history
git push --force origin feature  # now teammates are in trouble
```

---

## Common Workflows

**Option 1: Merge everything (GitHub default)**
```bash
git checkout main
git merge feature/login
# Preserves all history, shows merge points clearly
```

**Option 2: Rebase then merge (clean history)**
```bash
git checkout feature/login
git rebase main          # update with latest main
git checkout main
git merge feature/login  # now fast-forward, no merge commit needed
```

**Option 3: Squash merge (one commit per feature)**
```bash
git merge --squash feature/login
git commit -m "Add login feature"
# Collapses all feature commits into one
```

---

## Practical Recommendation

- **Daily workflow:** `rebase` to keep your local feature branch updated with main
- **Finishing a feature:** `merge` (or squash merge) into main
- **Cleaning up before PR:** `rebase -i` to squash/reorder your commits
- **Shared branches:** always `merge`, never `rebase`

The teams that get into trouble are usually those who rebase inconsistently or rebase shared branches — pick a convention and stick to it.
